title: India Is Running Out of Cancer Drugs. The Iran War Made Platinum Too Expensive.
excerpt: Cisplatin and carboplatin shortages are forcing patients to hunt across cities for their next dose as drugmakers halt production over price caps that no longer cover costs.
body:
Kumar Ajit spent more than a week calling dozens of pharmacies across India before he found the one drug his 70-year-old mother needed to keep fighting liver cancer. The drug was cisplatin, a platinum-based chemotherapy agent that has been a mainstay of oncology wards for decades. He eventually tracked it down in New Delhi and had it shipped to his village in Bihar — but not in the dosage she needed.

"I could not even get the desired dosage," the 52-year-old bank employee told Reuters. "I'm unsure what I will do for the next dose."

He is not alone. Across India, patients prescribed platinum-based chemotherapy drugs — cisplatin, carboplatin, and oxaliplatin — are scrambling for supplies as hospitals, particularly government-run ones, run dangerously low. Drug distributors in Hyderabad report fielding ten or more calls a day from patients desperately seeking cisplatin. And the crisis is accelerating.

## The War Premium on a Life-Saving Metal

The shortage traces directly to platinum, the rare metal at the heart of these chemotherapy drugs. Global platinum prices have surged over the past year, driven by constrained mine supply from South Africa, robust investment demand, and Middle East conflict disrupting supply chains. The Iran war — now in its fourth month — has compounded every pressure point.

Platinum prices in India have jumped from roughly ₹2,000 per gram to ₹5,000 per gram in the past year, according to Mohan Jain, a director at Naprod Life Sciences, one of India's specialist oncology drugmakers. That 150% increase has made production economically unviable under existing government price caps.

"The shortage is primarily driven by a steep increase in platinum prices," Jain said. Naprod has temporarily halted production of cisplatin and carboplatin altogether.

Rajiv Singhal, general secretary of the All India Organisation of Chemists and Druggists — a body representing 1.24 million members — confirmed the crisis has deepened sharply. "There has been a supply crunch for two months, but it has become worse over the last two weeks with a shortage," he said. "Drug distributors have been calling us complaining that they're not getting these drugs."

## A Quarter of Chemo Patients Affected

Doctors estimate that at least 25% of India's chemotherapy patients are on platinum-based regimens. These drugs treat cancers of the lung, ovaries, gall bladder, head and neck, and several other organs. There are few alternatives, and substitutes can be less effective or more toxic.

"They have been a backbone for cancer treatment," said Mintu Mathew Abraham, a consultant oncologist at PRS Hospital in Kerala. "Without them, it would be hard to continue treatment."

Venkateshwar Rao, an oncologist at Omega Hospital in Andhra Pradesh, echoed the concern, noting that for many cancers, platinum-based drugs are not a choice — they are the standard of care.

The manufacturers caught in the middle include some of India's largest generic drugmakers: Cipla, Intas Pharmaceuticals, and smaller oncology specialists like Naprod Life Sciences and Venus Remedies. All are constrained by the same math — raw material costs have outrun the prices they are allowed to charge.

## The Price Cap Trap

India's National Pharmaceutical Pricing Authority caps the retail price of essential medicines, including cisplatin and carboplatin. The intent is to keep life-saving drugs affordable. But when input costs spike beyond the cap, manufacturers face a brutal choice: produce at a loss or stop producing.

Venus Remedies, which supplies government hospitals, said it has absorbed losses for months but is now pulling back. "If those caps are not adjusted in line with rising costs, the supply chain comes under pressure," said Executive Director Saransh Chaudhary. "Companies cannot absorb the full increase, so patients ultimately bear the impact and shortages persist."

Drugmakers have sought an increase of roughly 50% in the price caps. India's pharmaceuticals department has not responded to requests for comment.

## What This Means for the Diaspora

For millions of NRIs with aging parents and relatives in India, the drug shortage adds a new layer of anxiety to an already strained situation. The Iran war's impact on India — through oil prices, inflation, and now medical supply chains — is no longer abstract. It is showing up in hospital wards and pharmacy counters in Bihar, Kerala, Hyderabad, and Andhra Pradesh.

The shortage also exposes a structural vulnerability: India, the "pharmacy of the world" for generic drugs, remains deeply dependent on imported raw materials. When global supply chains buckle — whether from conflict, sanctions, or price shocks — that dependence translates directly into empty shelves at home.

With no resolution to the Iran conflict in sight and platinum prices expected to remain elevated, oncologists warn the situation could worsen before it improves. For patients like Kumar Ajit's mother, the next dose remains an open question.
